title: How Body Dysmorphic Disorder Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a compulsive preoccupation with imagined or slight flaws in one's appearance. They cover the abbreviation and alternate name dysmorphophobia, prevalence (about one percent estimated, likely underdiagnosed), comorbidities such as OCD, anorexia and clinical depression, and symptoms like mirror checking, reassurance seeking, camouflaging, excessive grooming and dieting, and suicidal thoughts or self-harm. The hosts discuss why cosmetic surgery often fails for BDD sufferers, a small brain-imaging study on visual processing, the serotonin reuptake theory and SSRIs, cultural and media influences, muscular body dysmorphia, childhood maltreatment, and treatments including SSRIs and cognitive behavioral therapy. The episode closes with listener mail correcting a pronunciation of basalt, a reply about DC power transmission, and a wireless electricity suggestion.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke around, including Josh's childhood as a chubby kid and Chuck's comparisons, and introduce body dysmorphic disorder.

segments.title: What BDD is and who has it
segments.summary: The hosts define BDD as preoccupation with flaws, note the BDD and dysmorphophobia names, estimate about one percent prevalence likely underdiagnosed, and list comorbid conditions such as OCD, anorexia and depression.

segments.title: Reluctance to seek help and cosmetic surgery
segments.summary: People with BDD may hide symptoms from therapists and seek cosmetic surgery, which often does not relieve the condition and can lead to obsession shifting to other body parts or anger at surgeons.

segments.title: Symptoms and behaviors
segments.summary: The hosts go through symptoms: mirror checking or avoidance, comparing to others, excessive grooming, measuring, changing clothes, refusing photos, seeking reassurance, camouflaging flaws, anxiety around people, excessive dieting and exercise.

segments.title: Suicidal thoughts and self-harm
segments.summary: They discuss that roughly eight percent of those diagnosed have reported considering suicide and some have tried it, and that some people with BDD perform self-surgery on themselves.

segments.title: Biological theories: brain imaging and serotonin
segments.summary: A small study of about twenty-five people used MRI and face images to suggest BDD sufferers process visual detail with the left hemisphere. The hosts then explain tryptophan, serotonin and reuptake, and how SSRIs help BDD, suggesting a chemical imbalance.

segments.title: Cultural and media influences, childhood factors
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether media and magazine images contribute, note the condition was documented in the 1800s, mention muscular body dysmorphia, and cite a study where seventy percent of participants reported childhood maltreatment.

segments.title: Treatment
segments.summary: Treatments mentioned are SSRIs and cognitive behavioral therapy, which focuses on thoughts as the root of behavior and feelings. Quitting smoking and not eating is also said to help. The hosts advise seeking a therapist.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Corrections and suggestions: a basalt pronunciation correction, a reply about DC power transmission, and a suggestion for an episode on wireless electricity. Closing ad line.
